In the days of newspapers, headlines grabbed attention by telling you what the article was about. 'MAN BITES DOG', 'POLITICIAN CAUGHT IN SEX SCANDAL', 'OHIO NOW HAS 232 POLIO CASES'. This saved readers time - they bought the newspaper for a set price, and then read the parts of it that were interesting. Being honest and up-front about what was in each article made it easy to identify the things you were interested in and skim past the things that weren't.

It was also good for papers, because as long as they had one good story, you paid the full 'price of admission' to get the paper. In modern blogging/journalism, though, this breaks down. Since you don't pay an up-front fee to access content (some outlets have tried paywalls, but other than for academic sources these have proven unpopular), they have to generate revenue through ads. The more ads you see, the more money they make. That means they don't want you skimming through a list of descriptive headlines and only opening articles that are relevant to your interests, they want you to click on everything they post.

The 'good' way to get people to click on everything would be to provide lots of quality content. But that's hard. It's much easier to 'bait' people into clicking on things they wouldn't normally be interested in by throwing out mysteriously or ambiguously worded headlines, like the examples that have been given, to entice people to look at articles (and generate ad revenue) that they normally wouldn't.

The experience for the reader is kind of like being a kid on Christmas morning opening the biggest present just to find socks from Aunt Martha, though, and a lot of people are getting tired of it.
